newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary fears Czech crown crisis may hurt region.
newsitem.headline: Hungary fears Czech crown crisis may hurt region.

text.p: The Czech Republic needs to resolve its currency crisis soon to prevent a protracted struggle harming foreign investors' confidence in central Europe as a whole, Hungarian analysts said on Monday.
"If the (Czech) crisis and tension grows further, foreign capital may flow out of the region," said Gabor Oblath, analyst of the think-tank Kopint-Datorg.
"We saw in the (currency crises) case of Mexico (in 1995) that investors took out money from even those countries in Latin America where there was no problem with (economic) fundamentals."
The Czech central bank has intervened several times in the past two weeks to defend the crown, which was pushed to lows by a wave of short-sellings.
Some analysts predicted a radical devaluation in the near future to cut the soaring foreign trade deficit.

They said a substantial devaluation of the crown would be likely to lead to a flight of short-term investment capital from the Czech Republic, and part of that money would boost the markets of other countries of the region.
But they warned that for the longer term, the Czech currency crisis may harm the perception of central and eastern Europe by those investors who think only regionally.
"We are running together," said Judit Barta of GKI Economic Research. "We cannot rejoice that the former good boys are going bad now."
She said the Czech events have made it clear that the countries of the region should not be looked at as a bloc by investors as the economies were developing on different tracks.
"We (in Hungary) have just the opposite processes from those of the Czechs," said Barta.

She said that Hungary's economic growth was picking up, while the Czech GDP growth was slowing, and Hungary was about to phase out its imports surcharge by July while the Czech Republic took measures recently to make imports more expensive.

Other analysts said Hungary was on track towards sustainable GDP growth as economic reforms were more advanced than elsewhere in the region while the Czech delay in corporate sector reforms and high living standards weakened competitiveness there.
K&H Securities analyst Robert Rethy said the fall of the crown could make investors in central Europe more discerning.
"It will not influence capital investments in the region," Rethy said. "(But) perhaps foreign funds will have a more thorough look at where in the region they should put their money."
